$$
3\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+9y=7{e}^{x}+4{e}^{4x}
$$

has the complementary solution ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-3x}$, find the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ to this equation.

feedback.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation with constant coefficients on the left-hand side, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

We see that the right-hand side is $7{e}^{x}+4{e}^{4x},$ and neither ${e}^{x}$ nor ${e}^{4x}$ is a term in the complementary solution, so we assume a particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha {e}^{x}+\beta {e}^{4x},
$$

where $\alpha $ and $\beta $ are constants that are to be determined.

Calculating the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}{y}_{p}}{\text{d}x}=\alpha {e}^{x}+4\beta {e}^{4x}.
$$

To find the values of $\alpha $ and $\beta ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}3(\alpha {e}^{x}+4\beta {e}^{4x})+9(\alpha {e}^{x}+\beta {e}^{4x}) & =7{e}^{x}+4{e}^{4x} \\ (3\alpha +9\alpha ){e}^{x}+(12\beta +9\beta ){e}^{4x} & =7{e}^{x}+4{e}^{4x} \\ 12\alpha {e}^{x}+21\beta {e}^{4x} & =7{e}^{x}+4{e}^{4x}\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients of ${e}^{x}$ and ${e}^{4x},$ respectively, gives

$$
12\alpha =7\,\text{and}\,21\beta =4,
$$

So, we have

$$
\alpha =\frac{7}{12}\,\text{and}\,\beta =\frac{4}{21}.
$$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=\frac{7}{12}{e}^{x}+\frac{4}{21}{e}^{4x}.
$$
